newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Ciller warns of "cultural Berlin wall".
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Ciller warns of "cultural Berlin wall".

text.p: Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller called on the European Union on Thursday not to build a "cultural Berlin wall" against Moslem-populated Turkey by rejecting its bid for EU membership.

"Turkey is necessary for regional peace. To realise this peace... it is of utmost importance not to rebuild new cultural Berlin walls," Ciller told journalists and diplomats before a lunch for EU ambassadors.
Ankara received a further blow to its membership hopes this week when leading European Christian Democrats spoke out against inviting Turkey to join the union at a meeting in Brussels.
Ciller called on the EU to at least give Turkey the same treatment as other prospective members, mostly Eastern European.

"A new Europe where the same standards are applied to each country, will bring peace to the world," she said. "An environment where different criteria are applied to different countries, goes against the understanding of European democracy and human rights."

Ciller's pro-Western True Path Party and Turkey's secularist military, already coexisting uneasily with the Islamist-led coalition of Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, feel Turkey has not been rewarded for its loyalty to the West throughout the Cold War and, more recently, the Gulf War.

"We lost nearly 1,000 troops in Korea, we were there in time in Bosnia, we took our place in Iraq during the Gulf crisis... While engaged in this struggle, Turkey was there. But in 1997, at the reward for this struggle, Turkey is not there," she said.
The EU has kept Turkey at arm's length because of Ankara's human rights record, economic troubles and disputes with member Greece.
Many Turks feel the EU refuses to accept them because of historical and religious animosity.
"The European club really is a Christian club and they do not want Turkey in their midst because it is Moslem," columnist Mehmet Ali Birand wrote in the Sabah newspaper.
Turkey and the EU signed a customs union at the end of 1995 as part of an effort to forge a special relationship between Europe and the 60-million-strong country at Europe's southeastern rim.
